Our contributions are threefold.
(1) We formulate long-form writing for general-purpose agents as a process-level control problem and introduce a concrete system that chooses among planning, drafting, and reviewing during composition; (2) we compare our system with one-shot, fixed-stage, and adaptive task-planning alternatives across complementary long-form benchmarks; and (3) we use ablations and process analyses to locate the advantage in the shared process-level loop and characterize how the loop is used in practice.

replacements.before:
\condAgenticCogWriter\ reframes long-form writing for AI agents as process-level control: a top-level \texttt{Monitor} selects planning, drafting, or reviewing from persistent state and delegates to role-specific subagents.
Across three long-form writing benchmarks, our system is preferred to single-pass generation, fixed writing stages, and adaptive task planning in same-prompt comparisons; neither explicit goals nor adaptive process ordering alone explains the advantage, and most traces follow a simple planning--drafting--reviewing path.
These results support process-level control for long-form writing agents and show how cognitive writing theory yields executable, falsifiable hypotheses.
replacements.after:
\condAgenticCogWriter\ reframes long-form writing for AI agents as process-level control: a top-level \texttt{Monitor} selects planning, drafting, or reviewing from persistent state and delegates to role-specific subagents.
Across three long-form writing benchmarks, our system is preferred to single-pass generation, fixed writing stages, and adaptive task planning in same-prompt comparisons; ablations without explicit goals or with a fixed process order keep most of the advantage, and most traces follow a simple planning--drafting--reviewing path.
These results support process-level control for long-form writing agents and show how cognitive writing theory can be turned into control designs that are implemented and compared directly.
